title: CRAN Fedora check failures: system libnng 1.12.x has no working TLS
description:
Since late August, CRAN's r-devel Fedora flavors (`fedora-gcc`, `fedora-clang`) fail on nanonext 1.10.2:

-   **examples**: `tls_config()` errors with `9 | Not supported`
-   **tests**: process abort (`pthread_mutex_lock: Invalid argument` in `nng_aio_free`) during `ncurl("http://www.cam.ac.uk/", follow = TRUE)`

**Root cause**

Fedora updated its `nng` system package 1.9.0 → 1.12.2 on 2026-08-23. The [Fedora spec](https://src.fedoraproject.org/rpms/nng/raw/rawhide/f/nng.spec) builds with `-DNNG_TLS_ENGINE=openssl`, but NNG 1.12 removed the OpenSSL engine (only `mbed`/`wolf` remain), so the flag is silently ignored: the library is compiled with `NNG_SUPP_TLS` yet no engine is ever registered, and `nng_tls_config_alloc()` returns `NNG_ENOTSUP` at runtime.

Fedora's previous nng (1.9.0) was below our ≥ 1.12.0 minimum, so configure always compiled the bundled NNG there. The update made a TLS-less system libnng eligible for linking — the first time this configuration reached CRAN. Not a 1.10.2 regression; any nanonext ≥ 1.10.0 would fail identically.

title: `ncurl()` crash (double free) when following a redirect whose target fails to initialize
description:
Reported by CRAN checks: `r-devel-linux-x86_64-fedora-{clang,gcc}` ERRORs on nanonext 1.10.2 — the test run aborts with:
```
panic: pthread_mutex_lock: Invalid argument /lib64/libnng.so.1(nng_aio_free+0x1a) nanonext.so(...)
```
### Root cause

In `rnng_ncurl()` (`src/ncurl.c`), the aio is freed after a successful transaction but the pointer is not reset. When a redirect is followed, the
second pass through `relocall` can fail in `nng_http_client_alloc()` — before `nng_aio_alloc()` re-assigns `aio` — and the `fail:` cleanup then frees the dangling pointer again.

The CRAN failures were triggered by an environment change: Fedora updated its system libnng to 1.12.2 built without a working TLS engine, so following the 301 to `https://` fails client allocation with `NNG_ENOTSUP` and hits this path. The bug itself is long-standing and platform-independent, although previously difficult to trigger.

title: Double free in `rnng_dial()` when a blocking TLS dial fails
description:
## Symptom

Flaky `double free or corruption (out)` + SIGABRT (occasionally a segfault instead) in processes making TLS connections. Observed as mirai daemon crashes in the mirai test suite (~5/6 full-suite runs); the crashing process was confirmed via core dump to be `mirai::daemon("tls+tcp://...")`.

## Root cause

In the TLS branch of `rnng_dial()` (src/comms.c), the parsed URL is freed by the success-path `nng_url_free(up)` but the pointer is not NULLed. If the subsequent `nng_dialer_start()` fails — e.g. connection refused on a blocking dial (`autostart = NA`) — `goto fail` frees `up` a second time.

Core backtrace: `nni_url_free` (nng/src/core/url.c:448) ← `rnng_dial` (comms.c) ← R evaluation of `mirai::daemon()`.

title: Support incremental asynchronous HTTP response bodies
description:
Hi, and thank you again for this great library, which I have also used as inspiration for other NNG-based projects!

This issue follows the closed draft PR https://github.com/r-lib/nanonext/pull/328. The rough draft is currently used in [Rho](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/Rho) to determine whether nanonext can support the required semantics directly. I do not have the full context to determine the most consistent API level within nanonext, which is the main reason for opening this issue.

Rho needs to consume SSE responses from model providers while the HTTP response remains open, so that text deltas, reasoning updates, and tool calls can be emitted as they arrive and a later pending receive can be cancelled. `ncurl_aio()` currently resolves only after the complete transaction. The same requirement applies more generally to NDJSON, progressive downloads, and other long-lived response bodies.

Rho already uses nanonext Aios as its asynchronous I/O substrate, and uses mirai, which itself builds on nanonext, for worker execution. `rho.async` maps nanonext Aios into its task, stream, promise, and cancellation contracts. Using `httr2` for HTTP is a viable alternative: its connection interface supports pull-based streaming and nonblocking body reads. However, its promise interface resolves complete responses rather than individual streaming reads. Integrating its streaming connection into Rho would therefore require a separate curl readiness and cancellation adapter, or a blocking stream loop in a mirai worker with chunks relayed back to the main process. Both are possible, but they introduce a second transport lifecycle beside the existing nanonext Aio integration. The prototype was intended to find out whether nanonext could express these semantics directly instead.

At the nanonext level, the capability I am looking for is an asynchronous operation that makes the response status and headers available before the body completes, followed by cancellable asynchronous receives of raw response-body bytes with an explicit completion indication and close operation. HTTP framing and dechunking would remain in nanonext, while SSE and other application protocols would remain with the caller.

NNG exposes connection-level HTTP operations for connecting, writing the request, reading the response head, and then reading body bytes asynchronously. That seems like a possible implementation direction. I am unsure whether the resulting capability should extend `ncurl_aio()` and the existing Aio/stream interfaces, or use a separate low-level HTTP body handle. I would appreciate guidance on whether this belongs in nanonext and, if so, which direction would be most consistent with the existing API.

title: macOS sendmsg/readv EINVAL for large iov
description:
On macOS (XNU kernel), `sendmsg()` and `readv()` return `EINVAL` when the total bytes across all iov entries exceeds `INT_MAX` (2,147,483,647). This is a kernel-level constraint — the XNU socket layer uses 32-bit signed integers internally for aggregate iov size calculations.

NNG's POSIX transport layer passes iov lengths directly from the SP transport without capping. For messages larger than ~2 GiB (e.g. a
serialized R double vector of 3e8 elements = 2.4 GiB), the body iov_len exceeds `INT_MAX`. Combined with the 8-byte NNG framing header, the total exceeds the kernel limit, and the syscall fails.

The failure is silent from the caller's perspective: `nng_sendmsg()` returns 0 because the pair protocol completes the application AIO immediately upon accepting the message. The EINVAL occurs asynchronously in the I/O thread, which closes the pipe. The receiver then either times out or gets a connection error.

title: Performance of TLS encryption with a small number of small tasks
description:
### Discussed in https://github.com/shikokuchuo/nanonext/discussions/26
Originally posted by **wlandau** January 2, 2024 Hi @shikokuchuo, I hope you enjoyed your holidays! Since `mirai` and `nanonext` are more robust than ever, I find myself thinking about performance, specifically when it comes to TLS encryption. On my local Ubuntu machine, the following example with 100 tasks and TLS encryption takes almost 9 seconds to complete. I notice similar encryption-specific overhead when testing `crew.aws.batch` using real-life AWS Batch jobs. ```r library(nanonext) # 0.11.0.9005 library(mirai) # 0.11.3.9003 daemons(n = 1L, dispatcher = TRUE, url = host_url(ws = TRUE, tls = TRUE)) url <- rownames(status()$daemons) cv <- nextget("cv") cv2 <- cv() cv %~>% cv2 system(launch_remote(url = url), wait = FALSE) msleep(5000) n <- 1e2 start <- proc.time()["elapsed"] tasks <- replicate(n, mirai(TRUE)) while (cv_value(cv) < n) { until_(cv2, 500) } lapply(tasks, unresolved) elapsed <- unname(proc.time()["elapsed"] - start) daemons(n = 0L) print(elapsed) ``` When I turn off encryption, the same workload completes in under a tenth of a second. ```r library(nanonext) # 0.11.0.9005 library(mirai) # 0.11.3.9003 daemons(n = 1L, dispatcher = TRUE) url <- rownames(status()$daemons) cv <- nextget("cv") cv2 <- cv() cv %~>% cv2 launch_local(url = url) msleep(2000) n <- 1e2 start <- proc.time()["elapsed"] tasks <- replicate(n, mirai(TRUE)) while (cv_value(cv) < n) { until_(cv2, 500) } lapply(tasks, unresolved) elapsed <- unname(proc.time()["elapsed"] - start) daemons(n = 0L) print(elapsed) ``` I know there is inevitable overhead from encryption/decryption and maybe extra steps in the handshake, but I would not have expected the slowdown to be quite this much, especially given how fast HTTP and HTTPS both load web pages. You may already know where the bottleneck comes from, but I set up a quick profiling study anyway using `gperftools` and a few modifications in https://github.com/wlandau/nanonext/commit/dda175d86db9b2705937c2a23e743d0d8e6e70d0: ```r library(nanonext) # my fork library(mirai) # 0.11.3.9003 daemons(n = 1L, dispatcher = TRUE, url = host_url(ws = TRUE, tls = TRUE)) url <- rownames(status()$daemons) cv <- nextget("cv") cv2 <- cv() cv %~>% cv2 system(launch_remote(url = url), wait = FALSE) msleep(5000) n <- 1e2 samples <- tempfile() profiler_start(path = samples) tasks <- replicate(n, mirai(TRUE)) while (cv_value(cv) < n) { until_(cv2, 500) } daemons(n = 0L) profiler_stop() proffer::serve_pprof(pprof = samples) ``` Unfortunately the flame graph is not useful. Looks like either a standard library function or system call is taking the most time, or the bottleneck comes from a non-interactive external process or thread. ![pprof](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/nanonext/assets/1580860/c6ae07fb-e1d7-4a5b-a4f7-e9508ee06f17)

description:

title: Wait on multiple condition variables?
description: I really like `nextget("cv")` in `mirai`, and I think it could make polling in `targets` more gentle. However, in `crew`, there is a feature called [controller groups](https://wlandau.github.io/crew/articles/groups.html) which aggregates multiple controllers under a single interface. This feature meets the request from https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/discussions/28 for heterogeneous workers. Each controller in the controller group has its own condition variable, and it would be great to be able to wait until at least one of these condition variables gets signaled.

title: Condition variables to reduce polling in crew
description:
`nextget("cv")` and `mirai(.signal = TRUE)` are incredibly useful. We have already discussed `cv_value(nextget("cv"))` as a constant-time way to count unresolved tasks (https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/discussions/78#discussioncomment-7148551). Development `crew` already does this.

Now, I am thinking of ways that `nextget("cv")` could reduce polling in both `crew` and `targets`. There is a ton of potential. The crux is where `crew` either:

* Waits until at least one task resolves, or
* Waits until all tasks resolve.

I would like to use something like `until(nextget("cv"))`. It's simple in theory, but I find myself struggling:

1. `until()` decrements the cv. This is a challenge because `crew` thinks `cv_value(nextget("cv"))` is total cumulative number of resolved tasks. To use the cv correctly for https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mirai/discussions/78#discussioncomment-7148551, I have to add back 1 if the cv was originally positive. And it's hard to tell if the cv was originally positive without hitting a race condition.
2. `until()` only sleeps if `cv_value()` is positive. I am not sure how to wait until all tasks resolve. It would be easier if the sleep could start at any value and simply wait for a change. If there were a way to wait until the cv climbs up to a user-defined fixed positive value, then this would be easier still.

title: Trouble using until()
description:
I am trying to use `mirai::nextget("cv")` in `controller$wait()` and `controller$map()` in `crew` in order to avoid the worst aspects of polling. But I am finding that `nanonext::until()` somehow decrements the condition variable. This leaves me with the unfortunate choice of (1) do not wait on `nextget("cv")` as I would like to do in #17, or (2) go back to the inefficient way of counting unresolved tasks (i.e. revert https://github.com/wlandau/crew/issues/131) because `cv_value(nextget("cv"))` can no longer be trusted to count resolved ones. Reprex:

```r
library(mirai)
library(nanonext)
url <- "ws://127.0.0.1:5700"
daemons(n = 1L, url = url)
launch_local(url = url)
cv <- nextget("cv")
cv_value(cv)
#> [1] 0
task <- mirai(TRUE, .signal = TRUE)
Sys.sleep(0.25)
cv_value(cv)
#> [1] 1
task <- mirai(Sys.sleep(1), .signal = TRUE)
until(cv, 2000)
cv_value(cv) # I would expect 2.
#> [1] 0
daemons(n = 0L)
```

title: System endianness bug affecting nanonext 0.9.2
description:
`nanonext` 0.9.2 brought performance enhancements to serialisation / unserialisation by moving this to a lower level.

Part of the gains was to allow use of system endianness for serialisation, which is fine as unserialisation can automatically account for this. So this is not an issue even for sending/receiving between systems with different endianness.

However the same underlying functions were adopted by the sha / base64 functions, which *is* now problematic as the output will differ depending on system endianness.

title: nanonext is mutating the `NA` value shared across all R packages
description:
Originally reported at https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/issues/265.

Expected behaviour:

```r
fn <- function() NA
fn <- compiler::cmpfun(fn)

attributes(fn())
#> NULL
```

Unexpected:

```r
library(nanonext)
s <- socket(dial = "inproc://nano")
r <- recv_aio(s)
r$data

attributes(fn())
#> $class
#> [1] "unresolvedValue"
```

This is a critical bug that breaks all sorts of things in other packages (for instance `devtools::load_all()` fails after that).

The problem occurs here: https://github.com/shikokuchuo/nanonext/blob/2dfe7e6dfbb7d49eebc49686a9f13268fd65e73c/src/aio.c#L276-L277. Before using mutating functions like `classgets()`, you should check that you own the object. `ScalarLogical()` returns shared objects. You can `duplicate()` before setting the class to fix this. Note that there is also a protection error, you should protect the result of `mkString()` before calling `classgets()` since the latter allocates, which triggers GC.

Unrelatedly, since S3 classes are not namespaced, you should in principle soft-namespace all S3 classes with your package name. For instance the `nanoContext` class belongs in principle to the `nano` package. A proper class name for your package would be `nanonextContext`.
